full_judgment:
3. The trial Court decreed the suit. Relying on Abdul Gafur Sardar and ors. Vs. Wazed AIi Talukdar and another, 19 DLR 33 (37) wherein it is observed that "the Mukti-patra cannot confer the title on any party unless it is supported by a registered deed of transfer-kabala or gift" the trial Court held that the deed of release was not a document of transfer and that plaintiff No. 1 was the real owner of the property. The Appellate Court, however, reversed that decision. It disbelieved the case of benami on a detailed considerations of matters involved in the case. There was no evidence as to the necessity of the benami purchase. The plaintiffs did not produce the original document, namely, the sale certificate. The kabuliyat, Ext. 1, by Afsar and others, was executed on 2nd May, 1939 in favour of Krishna Lal Kundu indicating that even in 1939 the plaintiff was not acknowledged as the real owner of the lands. Exhibits-2 series show that some land was recorded in the name of Afsar. From 1931, the year of auction purchase, till 1948, the year plaintiff No. 2 obtained the ex parte decree in the rent suit against Afsar and others, impleading plaintiff No. 2 as a proforma-defendant, there was nothing to show that the lands were acquired by plaintiff No. 1. The assertions of the plaintiffs in the plaint and in the release are at variance. In the release it is stated that plaintiff No. 2 was the benamder, but the plaint indicated that plaintiff No. 2's father Krishna Lal was the benamder. In the plaint it was stated that plaintiff No. 1 was the real auction purchaser, but Exhibit-A, the written objection filed by plaintiff No. 2 before the Additional Deputy Commissioner, showed that the father of plaintiff No. 1 was the auction-purchaser. Plaintiff No. 1 and his father could not be the auction-purchaser at one and the same time as much as plaintiff No. 2 and his father could not be the benamder at the same time. The land acquired in rent execution case in 1931 was far in excess of the suit land, and plaintiff No. 1 did not take the deed of release in respect of the entire suit land claimed to have been purchased by him. The Appellate Court construed the release as an instrument of transfer. 

 "It was brought to the notice of Government that in some areas the land-holders were selling out or otherwise transferring all kinds of lands including waste lands in their khas possession on a large scale with a view to get a greater benefit out of the provisions of the East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Bill 1948, when enacted and put into operation. It was apprehended that if such transfers were allowed to go on unrestricted, the land-holders would dispose of their excess khas lands leaving little land to be acquired by Government under the proposed State Purchase Scheme, for distribution among agriculturists having no land or possessing uneconomic holdings. It was, therefore, considered necessary that immediate steps should be taken to restrict such transfers of khas lands on a large scale." 

 6. The case of Mt. Goday Koowur Vs. Mt. Ladoo, 13 Moor Ind App 585 (PC), is the earliest authority of note for the proposition that a bare admission in a document, made without any consideration, that the executant has no interest in a property, cannot pass his subsequently acquired title to the property. In that case it was held that a petition admitting that the petitioner has no claim to a certain estate did not operate as a conveyance of the subsequently acquired title, the petition having been filed in a pending suit by a petitioner having no present interest in the estate with a view to avoid an objection as to want of parties, and without receiving any consideration for the transfer of her future title. 

 It may be pointed out here that no such issue of benami was framed by the trial Court as there was no material proposition with regard to the question of benami before the trial Court. It appears that the lower appellate Court suo motu raised this issue of fact as to benami for the first time in the appellate Court when as a matter of fact this issue was not specifically raised in the trial Court nor any evidence was adduced by the parties in respect of benami. The land of plaintiff No. 1 having been forfeited by the Government, the plaintiffs asserted in the plaint that by virtue of the deed of release the defendant-Government cannot forfeit the land as this document was not a document of transfer. The Government's main contention in the written statement was that this deed of release was a document of transfer and the land stood forfeited to the Government. In view of the pleadings, it is really unfortunate that when no issue of benami was specifically mooted before the trial Court, the appellate Court went beyond its jurisdiction to frame an issue of fact at the appellate stage which was not at all taken up at the trial stage. Further, I may point out here that both the real owner and the ostensible owner filed the suit together for a declaration that the forfeiture of the land is not valid and legal in view of the deed of release Ext. 7. Thus, it is difficult to appreciate how the question of benami was relevant and a material proposition within the frame of the suit. The lower appellate Court without applying its mind to the real question of fact in issue as settled by the trial Court illegally decided the issue of benami in the present case when as a matter of fact no evidence was adduced by either side on the question of benami in the suit. I may point out that an issue of fact must be confined to the real question in controversy. Here the real question is, whether the defendant can forfeit the land of plaintiff No. 1 on the basis of transfer by Ext. 7. The mere reference of benami in the plaint and the denial of the same by the defendant in the written statement does not make the question of Benami a material question for the purpose of framing an issue at the appellate stage. Consequently, the lower appellate Court's judgment on this point is erroneous and not sustainable in law. 

 31. It is to be stated that deed of release is not a primary document of transfer. Consequently, I am called upon to consider this document as a whole, particularly from the operative portion of the document as to whether the same can be construed as a transfer as defined in the said Act though this registered instrument is styled as a deed of release.
